summary.text: Surface tension is the energy per unit area that comes from a liquid having a surface, and it can equally be given as a force per unit length.
Molecules at the surface do not have neighbours on all sides, so they are pulled inward and liquid surfaces contract to the minimum area.
Water's web of hydrogen bonds gives it a higher surface tension than most liquids, which lets razor blades and insects float on its surface.

facts.label: Units
facts.value: Force per unit length, or energy per unit area

facts.label: Drop shape
facts.value: Water droplets are pulled toward a sphere

facts.label: Force definition
facts.value: γ = F/2L, since the film has two sides

items.prompt: An insect denser than water rests on a pond without sinking even partly. What lets it do so?

options.label: The strong attraction among water molecules gives the surface a high tension
The insect's weight spreads evenly, so water cannot push back at all
Water repels anything denser than itself at the surface
The pond's depth stops the insect from sinking

items.explain: Water's molecules attract each other strongly through hydrogen bonds, giving it a high surface tension that lets denser objects float on its surface.

items.prompt: Why is a molecule at the surface of a liquid pulled inward, while one deep inside is not?

options.label: Surface molecules are heavier than those deeper down
Air above the surface pushes each molecule down strongly
Surface molecules carry a charge that the others lack
It has no neighbours on one side, so the pulls do not balance

items.explain: A molecule inside is pulled equally in every direction, giving a net force of zero, while surface molecules lack neighbours on all sides and are pulled inward.

items.prompt: Why is detergent added to wash water to help it reach the material being cleaned?

options.label: It makes the water molecules attract each other more
It lowers the water's surface tension, so there is more contact
It thickens the water so that it clings to the material
It heats the water so that it spreads more easily

items.explain: Surfactants such as detergents reduce surface tension so there is more contact between the liquid and another material.

items.prompt: A free-floating drop of liquid with no other forces acting on it ends up round. Why?

options.label: Air pressure squeezes it evenly into a ball
Its molecules repel one another until they spread out evenly
A sphere has the least surface area for its volume, so the least energy
Gravity pulls its sides inward at the same rate

items.explain: Mechanical systems seek minimum potential energy, and a sphere has the minimum surface area for a given volume.

items.prompt: In a glass, water curves up at the wall, while mercury curves down. What decides which curve a liquid takes?

options.label: How strongly it clings to itself versus the glass
Which of the two liquids is the denser one
How warm the room happens to be that day
How wide the glass is at the top

items.explain: The balance between the liquid's cohesion and its adhesion to the container determines the wetting, contact angle and meniscus shape.

items.prompt: A soap film stretched on a frame pulls on the movable bar from both of its faces. How does this change the way its tension is worked out from the measured force?

options.label: The force is doubled, since two faces pull twice as hard
The force is ignored and only the bar's length is used
The force is squared, since the film has two faces
The force is divided by twice the length, since each face shares it

items.explain: The film has two surfaces that each contribute equally to the force, so the tension is defined as γ = F/2L.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Surface tension is the energy per unit area that a liquid has because it has a surface. It can be expressed either as a force per unit length or as an energy per unit area, and the two are equivalent. When speaking of energy per area, people often use the term surface energy, which is broader because it applies to solids too. Surface tension is the term used for liquids.

paragraphs.heading: Why surfaces pull inward
paragraphs.text: Molecules of the same kind attract each other through what are called cohesive forces. A molecule deep inside a liquid is pulled equally in every direction by its neighbours, so the net force on it is zero. A molecule at the surface does not have equal numbers of neighbours on all sides, so it is pulled inward. That inward pull makes liquid surfaces contract to the smallest possible area. Separately, cohesive forces between the molecules produce a tension running along the surface where liquid meets air, and that tension resists a push from outside.

paragraphs.heading: The energy picture
paragraphs.text: The same idea can be described in terms of energy. A molecule touching a neighbour has lower energy than one on its own. Molecules at the boundary are missing some neighbours, so they have higher energy than those inside. To keep its energy as low as possible, a liquid keeps the number of boundary molecules to a minimum, which means a minimal surface area and a smooth shape.

paragraphs.heading: Why drops are round
paragraphs.text: Surface tension gives liquid droplets their shape. Water drops deform easily, yet the imbalance in cohesive forces at their surface pulls them toward a sphere. With no other forces acting, drops of virtually any liquid would be roughly spherical. A sphere has the smallest surface area for a given volume, a point first made by Gibbs.

paragraphs.heading: Water stands out
paragraphs.text: Water molecules attract each other strongly through a web of hydrogen bonds, which gives water a higher surface tension than most liquids: 72.8 millinewtons per metre at 20 °C. This lets things denser than water, such as razor blades and water striders, rest on its surface without sinking in even partly. Surfactants, such as detergents, are used to lower surface tension so that a liquid makes more contact with another material.

paragraphs.heading: Wetting and the meniscus
paragraphs.text: Liquids also feel adhesive forces, the attraction between molecules of different kinds, such as a liquid and its container. The balance between cohesion and adhesion decides how well the liquid wets a surface, its contact angle and the shape of its meniscus. When cohesion wins, as with mercury in glass, wetting is low and the meniscus at a vertical wall is convex. When adhesion wins, as with water in glass, wetting is high and the meniscus is concave.
